ORIGINAL USMLE-STYLE PRACTICE

Unilateral throat swelling with trismus

A 17-year-old develops progressively severe right-sided throat pain over four days. He has a muffled voice, difficulty opening his mouth, and swelling above the right tonsil. The uvula points left. Which diagnosis best explains these findings?

  1. Right peritonsillar abscess
  2. Uncomplicated viral pharyngitis
  3. Acute epiglottitis
  4. Retropharyngeal abscess
  5. Infectious mononucleosis without a focal complication
Answer and explanation

Right peritonsillar abscess

A focal collection beside the tonsil displaces the palate and uvula; adjacent inflammation causes trismus.

Option explanations

Right peritonsillar abscess: A focal collection beside the tonsil displaces the palate and uvula; adjacent inflammation causes trismus.

Uncomplicated viral pharyngitis: Viral pharyngitis rarely produces this focal mass effect.

Acute epiglottitis: Epiglottitis produces supraglottic obstruction rather than unilateral tonsillar bulging.

Retropharyngeal abscess: A posterior deep-neck collection more often causes neck stiffness and posterior pharyngeal swelling.

Infectious mononucleosis without a focal complication: Mononucleosis often causes bilateral tonsillar enlargement and generalized adenopathy; it does not explain this focal pattern alone.
